principles.name: Wow our customers
principles.description: Customers are the center of ServiceNow's world; aim for the best customer experience and innovation, which includes listening closely and building lasting relationships, not only shipping products.
evidence_signals: Names a specific customer or internal user group, their pain, and how it was confirmed (feedback, tickets, data)
Went beyond the request to fix the underlying problem and can say what the customer gained
Measured the result in the customer's terms (time saved, tickets avoided, adoption, satisfaction)

principles.name: Win as a team
principles.description: Share the same goals, keep clear roles, deliver results together across functions, and enjoy the journey.
evidence_signals: Describes working across functions (product, engineering, sales, services) with a clear own role inside the team result
Shared credit and helped others succeed, not only their own piece
Resolved a disagreement so the team moved forward toward one goal

principles.name: Stay hungry and humble
principles.description: Do not take success for granted; stay ready to learn and evolve, bring fresh ideas, and keep ego out of the way.
evidence_signals: Owns a failure or mistake openly and shows the concrete change it led to
Learned a new domain or tool quickly to deliver, and keeps raising their own bar
Credits others and asks for feedback instead of defending their first idea

principles.name: Create belonging
principles.description: Lead with empathy: listen, respect each person's perspective, and make everyone feel they belong.
evidence_signals: Shows empathy in a story, for example understanding a colleague's or customer's position before acting
Made room for quieter or newer people and their ideas in a team
Helped a struggling colleague in a respectful, constructive way

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, projects, interest in ServiceNow and enterprise software, work persona and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Online coding assessment
rounds.notes: Reported as one or two coding problems plus multiple-choice CS fundamentals; more common for early-career roles. ServiceNow's hiring page confirms a coding assessment may be part of the process. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding interviews
rounds.notes: One or two live coding rounds (data structures and algorithms; Java or JavaScript common). Reported as 45 to 60 minutes. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Common for mid and senior roles: multi-tenant workflow, API, scheduler or notification design, plus build-versus-configure questions on the Now Platform. Some loops use low-level design instead. Duration is a common-pattern estimate.

rounds.name: Behavioral / values interview
rounds.interviewer_role: Engineer or manager from the hiring team
rounds.notes: STAR stories on customer impact, cross-team collaboration, conflict, trade-offs and failure, mapped to the four values. ServiceNow says it uses standard evaluation guides. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Past projects, ownership and level fit; sometimes includes a light technical or design question. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Motivation and fit with ServiceNow's platform direction. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Background, product experience, inbound versus outbound product work, and why ServiceNow. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Product sense / design
rounds.notes: Design or improve a Now Platform capability for admins, agents or employees, often balancing out-of-the-box features against custom configuration. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Analytical / execution
rounds.notes: Metrics for a feature (including GenAI features) and root-cause analysis of a metric drop. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Strategy and trade-offs
rounds.notes: Competitive position in a market and roadmap trade-offs such as a large customer's custom request versus the core roadmap. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Take-home and panel presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of PM, design, UX research and engineering
rounds.notes: Some teams ask for a case study presented to a cross-functional panel, with questions on how one solution was prioritized over another. Team-dependent. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Behavioral / values interview
rounds.notes: Customer focus, collaboration with engineering and sales, and handling disagreement. Duration is an estimate.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Quantitative background, models taken to production, interest in enterprise AI. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Statistics and ML fundamentals plus Python for data work. Only the verbal concepts part is simulated; the coding part is not.

rounds.name: Coding interview
rounds.notes: Candidates for ML engineering roles report coding-heavy loops (data structures and algorithms). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML deep dive
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior ML engineer or data scientist
rounds.notes: Model selection, features, evaluation and production ML; for Now Assist and generative AI teams, LLM and retrieval topics.

rounds.name: ML case study
rounds.notes: A ServiceNow-style business problem such as incident routing, request volume forecasting or knowledge article recommendation, including evaluation design.

rounds.name: Past project presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel from data science, product and engineering
rounds.notes: Candidate presents a past project end to end. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Behavioral interview
rounds.notes: Business impact of models, explaining results to non-technical stakeholders, failures and fairness trade-offs.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Team fit, roadmap, growth goals and mentoring.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Solution consultant (pre-sales) track: pre-sales history, product areas, territory. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: How the candidate runs a sales cycle with an account executive and wins technical evaluations.

rounds.name: Demo / technical presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel from sales, solution consulting and product
rounds.notes: Prepared mock demo or solution presentation tailored to a fictional prospect, with discovery and objection handling. Reported as the hardest stage. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Cross-functional panel
rounds.interviewer_role: Account executive, product manager and services lead
rounds.notes: Three short back-to-back conversations on working with sales, feeding field input to product, and handing off to services. Reported by one prep site.

rounds.name: Executive final
rounds.notes: Territory and vertical fit.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate went beyond what was asked for a customer or internal stakeholder, and how they knew it helped
A difficult client or user situation, such as saying no or delivering bad news, while keeping the relationship
A complex problem solved by working across teams or functions, and the candidate's own role in the shared result
A disagreement with a manager or peer, or a difficult co-worker, and how the candidate got to a shared way forward
A project or decision that failed, what the candidate owned, and what they changed afterwards
A time the candidate showed empathy, supported a struggling colleague, or made someone feel included
A difficult technical or product trade-off under time pressure, the options considered and how it turned out
Walk through a technical or product project the candidate led: the goal, the hardest part, own decisions and the result
Why ServiceNow and this team, and how the candidate's experience and values fit the platform and its customers
Design a workflow, scheduling or notification system that serves thousands of enterprise customers, covering isolation, scale and upgrades
When to use an out-of-the-box platform capability or configuration and when to write custom code, and the long-term cost of each

question_patterns.theme: ML and AI for service operations
question_patterns.pattern: Build and evaluate a model or AI feature for IT and service workflows, such as ticket routing, resolution prediction or an AI agent
Design or improve a platform feature for a specific enterprise user (admin, service agent, employee), choosing between out-of-the-box and custom
Define success metrics for a feature, including AI features, or diagnose a drop in adoption or usage
Decide on a large customer's custom request that competes with the core roadmap, or respond to a competitor in a market

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer or a stakeholder.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use STAR with most time on Action. Name the customer or internal user and the specific pain, with evidence of it. Explain what the candidate personally did beyond the normal scope and what it cost them or the team. Close with a result in the customer's terms (hours saved, fewer tickets, renewal or adoption) and how the relationship changed. Pitfalls: a story where 'above and beyond' means only long hours, or a team story with no 'I'.

looking_for: Whether you start from the customer's real problem
What you personally did beyond your normal scope
strong_signals: Evidence of the pain before acting
A result measured in the customer's terms
watch_outs: 'Above and beyond' meaning only long hours

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you worked with other teams to solve a complex problem.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set up why one team could not solve it alone and which teams were involved. Show the candidate's own role: aligning goals, clarifying who owns what, and keeping communication flowing. Describe one point of friction and how it was settled. End with the shared result and what the candidate would repeat. Pitfalls: all 'we' with no own contribution, or a story where other teams are the villains.

looking_for: How you align several teams on one goal
Your own role inside the shared result
strong_signals: Clear owners and goals set early
Handles one real point of friction well

sample_questions.question: What would you do if you had to tell a customer you cannot solve their problem?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show honesty early rather than stalling. Explain how the candidate confirms the request and the real need behind it, says clearly what is not possible and why, and offers the best alternative or workaround with a next step and owner. Add how they follow up and pass the feedback to product. A real past example makes this stronger. Pitfalls: overpromising, hiding behind policy, or ending the conversation without an alternative.

looking_for: Whether you are honest early with the customer
Whether you still find a way to help
strong_signals: Confirms the real need behind the request
Offers an alternative with a clear next step
watch_outs: Hiding behind policy with no alternative

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to work with a difficult co-worker.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the behavior, not the person, and its effect on the work. Show the candidate tried to understand the other side first, then had a direct, private conversation and agreed on how to work together. Explain what changed and how the relationship looks now. Strong answers show some self-reflection on the candidate's own part. Pitfalls: venting about the colleague, escalating first, or a story with no resolution.

looking_for: Whether you try to understand the other person first
How you get the work back on track
strong_signals: Talks about behavior and impact, not character
Reflects on your own part in the friction

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you failed.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real failure with real stakes. State clearly what the candidate owned, without blaming others or circumstances. Explain how they found out, what they did to recover, and the root cause. Show the lasting change in how they work, ideally with a later example where it helped. This probes humility and appetite to learn. Pitfalls: a disguised strength, a failure with no consequences, or no change afterwards.

looking_for: Whether you own your part honestly
What you learned and changed
strong_signals: A real failure with real stakes
A later example where the lesson helped

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you showed empathy and understanding at work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the other person's situation (a colleague, a new team member, a frustrated user) and how the candidate noticed it. Show listening and asking before acting, then a concrete action that helped, such as adjusting a plan, giving cover, or connecting them with support. End with the effect on the person and the work. Pitfalls: a vague story about being nice, or empathy that ignored the work's needs entirely.

looking_for: Whether you notice and understand others' situations
What concrete action you took
strong_signals: Listens and asks before acting
Shows the effect on the person and the work
watch_outs: A vague story about being nice

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a difficult technical trade-off you had to make.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out the options and the constraints (deadline, customer impact, maintainability, cost). Explain the criteria used, who was consulted, and why one option won. Be honest about what was given up and how that risk was managed later, for example with a follow-up task or monitoring. Close with how it turned out and what the candidate would decide now. Pitfalls: a trade-off with an obvious answer, or no mention of the cost of the chosen path.

looking_for: How you weigh competing options
Whether you name what you gave up
strong_signals: Clear criteria and the people consulted
Managed the risk of the chosen path
watch_outs: A trade-off with an obvious answer
No cost to the chosen option

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you explained complex analytical results to people without a technical background.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the audience and the decision they had to make. Show how the candidate led with the answer and its business meaning, used a simple visual or analogy, and was honest about uncertainty. Explain how they checked understanding and what decision followed. Pitfalls: walking through methods instead of the conclusion, hiding uncertainty, or blaming the audience for not understanding.

looking_for: Whether you lead with the decision and its meaning
How you handle uncertainty with a lay audience
strong_signals: Answer first, method later
Checks understanding and names the decision taken
watch_outs: Walking through methods instead of conclusions

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a presentation or demo that did not go well and what you learned from it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the audience, the goal, and what went wrong (wrong focus, a failed demo, an objection the candidate could not answer). Own the preparation gap honestly. Explain how they recovered in the room or after, and what they now do differently, such as deeper discovery or rehearsing failure paths. A later success using the lesson makes it strong. Pitfalls: blaming the audience or the technology.

looking_for: Whether you own the preparation gap
What you changed in how you prepare
strong_signals: Honest account of what went wrong
A later success using the lesson
watch_outs: Blaming the audience or the technology

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a technical project you led. What was hardest, and how did you handle it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give the goal, the team, and the candidate's exact role. Spend most time on the hardest part: the options, the decision, and how they brought others along. Include numbers for scale and outcome. Show level-appropriate scope: a component for mid-level, a system across teams for senior and above. End with what they would change. Pitfalls: listing tasks without decisions, or claiming the whole team's work.

looking_for: Your exact role and decisions
Whether the scope fits the level
strong_signals: Most time on the hardest part
Numbers for scale and outcome

sample_questions.question: Why does your background fit ServiceNow's move from a system of record to a platform that takes action with AI?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show real understanding of the platform: workflows across IT, employee and customer service, and the shift toward AI agents that act, not only record. Connect two or three concrete experiences (workflow products, enterprise customers, AI features) to that direction. Say what the candidate wants to learn and why this team. Pitfalls: generic praise, repeating marketing lines, or no link between own experience and the company's direction.

looking_for: Whether you understand the platform's direction
How your experience connects to it
strong_signals: Two or three concrete links to own experience
Says what you want to learn here
watch_outs: No link to your own experience

sample_questions.question: Design a workflow automation service that runs millions of workflow executions a day for thousands of enterprise customers.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify workflow shape (steps, approvals, waits, external calls), volume, latency and tenancy. Propose a definition store, a durable execution engine with persisted state, queues and workers, and timers for long waits. Cover idempotent steps and retries, per-tenant fairness and quotas so one customer cannot starve others, versioning of running workflows, observability and audit. Discuss trade-offs between shared and isolated infrastructure. Pitfalls: in-memory state, or ignoring noisy tenants.

looking_for: How you keep long-running workflows durable
How you isolate and share capacity between tenants
strong_signals: Idempotent steps with retries and timers
Per-tenant quotas and workflow versioning

sample_questions.question: Each customer has its own application layer and database. How would you scale, upgrade and isolate a fleet built that way?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the benefits (strong isolation, per-customer upgrades and data residency) and costs (fleet size, operations, uneven load). Cover automated provisioning, placement and capacity planning, rolling upgrades with canaries and rollback, schema migration across many databases, backup and restore, and fleet-wide monitoring. Discuss when to consolidate small tenants and how to handle a very large one. Pitfalls: manual operations, or one big-bang upgrade.

looking_for: Whether you see both benefits and costs of per-customer stacks
How you upgrade a large fleet safely
strong_signals: Canary and staged upgrades with rollback
Automated provisioning and fleet-wide monitoring

sample_questions.question: When would you use a built-in platform feature or configuration, and when would you write custom code instead?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Frame the decision around the customer's need and long-term cost. Prefer built-in features and configuration when they meet the need, because they upgrade cleanly and are easier for admins to own. Choose custom code when the need is truly unique or performance-critical, and contain it behind clear interfaces with tests. Mention upgrade risk, technical debt, governance and who maintains it. Give an example. Pitfalls: always custom for control, or forcing a built-in feature that does not fit.

looking_for: How you weigh fit today against upgrade cost later
Who will own and maintain the result
strong_signals: Defaults to configuration when it meets the need
Contains custom code behind clear interfaces
watch_outs: Forcing a feature that does not fit

sample_questions.question: How would you build a model that predicts how long an IT incident will take to resolve?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify how the prediction is used (routing, SLA alerts, customer expectations). Define the target carefully, including reopened and still-open tickets. Propose features from ticket text, category, priority, assignment group, history and time, and a baseline before more complex models. Cover leakage from fields set later, skewed durations, evaluation by segment, drift, and how predictions are shown to agents. Pitfalls: a single accuracy number, or features not known at prediction time.

looking_for: How you define the target and its use
Whether you avoid leakage and skew
strong_signals: Starts with a baseline model
Evaluates by segment and plans for drift
watch_outs: Features not known at prediction time
One accuracy number as the only metric

sample_questions.question: How would you evaluate, offline and online, an AI agent that resolves service requests end to end?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define success: correct resolution, safe actions, customer satisfaction and cost. Offline, build a labeled set of real requests, score task success and step correctness, and add checks for harmful or unauthorized actions; use human review or a calibrated model judge where labels are scarce. Online, start in shadow mode or with human approval, then A/B test on resolution rate, escalations, reopen rate, latency and cost, with guardrails and rollback. Pitfalls: judging only by fluent answers.

looking_for: How you define success beyond fluent answers
How you roll out an agent safely
strong_signals: Offline set with checks for unsafe actions
Shadow mode before A/B test, with guardrails
watch_outs: Judging only by how good answers sound

sample_questions.question: Design a platform feature that helps IT admins find and deal with unapproved software and services before they become a security risk.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify users (IT admin, security, the employee using the tool) and the goal (risk reduction without blocking work). Map how unapproved tools are found today and the main pains. Propose discovery from existing data (expense, network, single sign-on), a risk score, and workflows to approve, replace or retire, with employee-friendly messaging. Prioritize a first version, define metrics (time to detect, risky apps retired, employee friction) and say what stays out-of-the-box. Pitfalls: pure blocking.

looking_for: How you balance security with employee productivity
Which user you design for first
strong_signals: Uses data the platform already has
A scoped first version with clear metrics
watch_outs: Pure blocking that pushes people to hide tools

sample_questions.question: What metrics would show that a generative AI incident-summary feature really saves agents time?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with the goal: faster, better incident handling, not usage for its own sake. Propose a primary metric such as time to resolve or handle time for incidents with summaries versus without, measured through a controlled test. Add adoption, edits made to summaries, agent satisfaction, and quality guardrails (wrong summaries, escalations, reopen rate) plus cost per summary. Explain how to separate novelty effects. Pitfalls: counting summaries generated, or no comparison group.

looking_for: Whether you measure value, not activity
How you prove the effect is real
strong_signals: One primary time metric with a comparison group
Quality and cost guardrails

sample_questions.question: Use of the mobile app by field technicians dropped 15% in a month. How do you find out why?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Confirm the data first (tracking changes, definition of active user, seasonality). Segment by customer, region, device, app version and task type, and check the funnel from login to completed job. Look for internal causes (release, outage, login changes) and external ones (a large customer churned, fewer jobs, a competing tool). Rank hypotheses, say what data would confirm each, and give a short-term fix and longer-term action. Pitfalls: proposing features before locating the drop.

looking_for: Whether you validate the data first
How you segment to locate the drop
strong_signals: Checks internal and external causes
Ranks hypotheses with the data to test each
watch_outs: Proposing features before locating the drop

sample_questions.question: A Fortune 500 customer wants a valuable custom feature that would delay the core roadmap. How do you decide?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the customer's underlying need and whether others share it. Weigh revenue and relationship value against the cost of delay to many customers, upgrade and maintenance burden, and precedent. Look for options: meet the need with configuration, generalize it into the roadmap, or partner and services. Make a clear recommendation, how to communicate it to the customer and sales, and the decision rule for future requests. Pitfalls: yes to the biggest customer by reflex.

looking_for: How you weigh one customer against many
Whether you find options beyond yes or no
strong_signals: Checks whether other customers share the need
A clear recommendation and a rule for next time
watch_outs: Saying yes to the biggest customer by reflex

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Entry-level engineer who delivers well-defined tasks with guidance and writes tested code.
Owns features within a team from design to release with limited guidance.
Senior engineer who designs components or services, leads projects within a team and mentors others.
Staff engineer who leads design across several teams and drives technical decisions for a product area.
Sets technical direction for a large area, often leading a small group while still coding.
Principal engineer who shapes architecture across organizations and the platform.
Owns a product area on the platform and its metrics, working with engineering, design and field teams.
Sets strategy for a product line or workflow area and influences roadmaps across teams.

persona.tone: Warm, conversational and professional; interested in the person as well as the work
persona.pace: Moderate; two or three stories per behavioral round, with time to think before design answers
persona.pushback_style: Asks what the candidate did personally versus the team, how the customer benefited, and why one option beat the alternatives (including configure versus build); probes for what was learned
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions; no feedback in the room, the recruiter follows up after the team debrief

case_style.notes: Cases are enterprise B2B: users are admins, service agents and employees inside large customers. Expect out-of-the-box versus custom configuration trade-offs, metrics for generative AI features, root-cause analysis of adoption drops, and roadmap trade-offs against large customer requests. Market sizing is rare.

sources.title: ServiceNow Form 10-K FY2025: Our Ambition, Values and Corporate Purpose
ServiceNow product manager interview questions (JobMentis, public sample)
ServiceNow IC5 vs IC4 SWE (Blind discussion)

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the four value names come from ServiceNow's own blog series and FY2025 proxy and 10-K, and descriptions are paraphrased from the 10-K; the 2025 careers-page values graphic is an image we could not read, so check the current wording there. Weights are our estimate of interview emphasis.

loop_structure: ServiceNow's hiring page says only that rounds vary by role and may include a coding assessment or presentation; round lists come from prep sites and candidate reports. Most durations are common-pattern estimates. The PM rounds come mainly from one prep site, and the solution consultant (other) loop from one prep site.
question_patterns: sample questions come from prep sites that collect candidate reports (CleverPrep, JobMentis public sample, How2Become, TechPrep); no ServiceNow page lists interview questions.

bar_by_level: IC1 to IC6 and the IC3 Senior and IC4 Staff titles come from Levels.fyi; IC5 Senior Staff comes from a Blind thread, and Principal is reported as IC6 in postings but IC7 in one Blind post. PM level titles are unverified common titles, and scope text is our summary.
persona: no public source describes interviewer style beyond 'conversational' candidate reports and the official note on standard evaluation guides; tone and pushback are our estimate.
scoring_weights: derived from the values and from the signals prep sites list (collaboration, ownership, trade-offs, customer focus); no public source gives weights.
case_style: PM case themes come mostly from one prep site's public sample; the split between product sense and system thinking is our estimate.
